query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al), the ability to form and sustain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer above 900 °C is governed by the near‐surface partitioning of the minor alloying element. When the added element (particularly Al) partitions homogeneously to the surface and promotes the cooperative formation of a slow-growing, dense oxide (e.g., α-Al2O3 or Cr2O3), the oxide scale develops with low internal stresses and remains adherent. In contrast, if the microstructure is inhomogeneous (or if the minor element is Mn or Si), the oxide scale forms as mixed or ternary oxides with compositional gradients, which induces high stresses that crack or spall the scale.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution states
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation testing in air (or corrosive environments) at ~900–1000 °C; comparison against a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy without the minor X addition under identical thermal and atmospheric conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Local surface microstructure and element partitioning: a homogeneous near-surface enrichment (particularly of Al) that facilitates the nucleation of a continuous protective oxide layer versus the formation of heterogeneous, phase-separated oxide regions
generation.mechanism: Minor element addition alters the diffusional dynamics and elemental segregation during high-temperature exposure. When Al is present, its preferential segregation enables the formation of a slow-growing yet dense and coherent alumina (or cooperative Cr2O3) scale, which minimizes the thermal and intrinsic stresses. In alloys with Mn or Si, less stable mixed or ternary oxide phases develop due to uneven partitioning and phase separation, leading to stress accumulation, cracking, and spallation of the scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys containing Al (with a homogeneous, single-phase structure) will form and maintain a stable, coherent protective oxide layer during prolonged exposure above 900 °C, while alloys with Mn or Si, particularly if multiphase, will develop unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide scales. The baseline CrFeCoNi alloy is expected to form less protective, mixed oxide scales under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloy (without the X minor addition) under identical high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions
generation.boundary: Temperature above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres; applicable to both single-phase and multiphase metallic solid-solution states of CrFeCoNiX alloys
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of diffusion rates, local stress development, and phase boundaries in controlling oxide scale adhesion and spallation are not fully determined. Direct in situ characterization is required to resolve the detailed kinetics and spatial composition gradients.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-temperature synchrotron XRD and environmental TEM experiments on a series of CrFeCoNiX alloys (with X = Al, Mn, and Si) and a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy. Subject all samples to controlled oxidation in air at temperatures between 900 and 1000 °C. Track in real-time the nucleation, growth, and evolution of oxide phases, and monitor surface stress development and scale morphology.
measurements: Real-time phase identification and thickness measurement of oxide scales (e.g., detection of α-Al2O3, Cr2O3, or mixed oxides)
In situ observation of microstructure evolution and element partitioning at the surface (using TEM or high-resolution imaging)
Assessment of residual stresses and detection of cracking or spallation in the oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloys do not consistently form a continuous, low-stress, protective oxide scale distinct from that formed on Mn- or Si-containing and baseline alloys, or if the expected surface enrichment and segregation behavior are not observed, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

In this work, an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA was successfully fabricated through the arc-melting process, with an emphasis on phase, microstructure, and real-time oxidation behaviour in two different non-ambient (high-temperature and low-oxygen partial pressure) conditions. The main findings of this research work can be summarised as follows. In a vacuum (4.2 × 10−6 atm), only MnO, a halite-type oxide, was formed during in situ oxidation, contrary to ThermoCalc’s prediction of both halite and spinel oxides, and Ni/Co forming halite. In air (1.0 atm), vigorous oxidation was observed, with most of the oxides formed being spinel. Mn remained important in the formation of spinel oxides, and Co was predicted to form spinel oxides by ThermoCalc but was not found in oxide-forming elements. Oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, and Fe3O4 were not detected during in situ HTXRD in either vacuum or air, which contrasts with previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. Mn was found to be a higher oxide-forming element, producing non-protective oxides, and leading to the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy beneath the oxide layer. Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. AbstractTogether with the thermodynamics and kinetics, the complex microstructure of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) exerts a significant influence on the associated oxidation mechanisms in these concentrated solid solutions. To describe the surface oxidation in AlCoCrFeNi HEA, we employed a stochastic cellular automata model that replicates the mesoscale structures that form. The model benefits from diffusion coefficients of the principal elements through the native oxides predicted by using molecular simulations. Through our examination of the oxidation behavior as a function of the alloy composition, we corroborated that the oxide scale growth is a function of the complex chemistry and resultant microstructures. The effect of heat treatment on these alloys is also simulated by using reconstructed experimental micrographs. When they are in a single-crystal structure, no segregation is noted for α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3, which are the primary scale-forming oxides. However, a coexistent separation between Al2O3 and Cr2O3 oxide scales with the Al-Ni- and Cr-Fe-rich regions is predicted when phase-separated microstructures are incorporated into the model.Keywords: oxidation, high-entropy alloy,

decision.trend: Previous work on AlCoCrFeNi (PMC9498035) showed that protective oxide scale formation depends strongly on how alloying elements partition and affect oxide nucleation and growth at high temperature. Using a stochastic cellular automata model informed by molecular simulations, that study demonstrated that Al and Cr can cooperatively drive formation of thermodynamically stable, continuous oxides (e.g., α-Al2O3 or Cr2O3). However, local compositional inhomogeneities or phase-separated microstructures still lead to mixed or layered oxides prone to cracking and spallation. This underlines the broader challenge in CrFeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys of defining compositional and microstructural “windows” ensuring stable scales above about 900 °C.
decision.unsolved: Despite modeling insights, it remains unclear how variations in minor additions (e.g., Si, Mn, or Al) and the resulting microstructure transitions (e.g., from single-phase to multi-phase) alter oxide growth mechanisms in CrFeCoNiX alloys so that protective scales remain coherent and adherent during prolonged high-temperature exposure. In particular, direct real-time experimental validation of stress-driven oxide spallation or stable oxide adherence is still lacking.
decision.lever: Carry out high-temperature environmental TEM or synchrotron XRD on well-controlled CrFeCoNiX alloys (X = Si, Mn, Al) to monitor real-time oxide scale nucleation, growth kinetics, and spallation under cyclic oxidation up to ~1000 °C. Compare these observations to a baseline CrFeCoNi or Ni-based alloy system under identical conditions, tracking scale thickness, phase evolution, and residual stresses.
decision.why: Following the recent modeling work on AlCoCrFeNi (PMC9498035), in situ/operando experiments provide the most direct path to testing the central hypothesis: that emergent minor-element partitioning and local microstructure changes control whether a continuously protective oxide (e.g., α-Al2O3, Cr2O3) forms without cracking or spalling. Direct observation of surface-scale evolution and stress states is essential to confirm or refute model predictions and to identify the underlying conditions that yield stable versus unstable oxide layers.
